content: The findings of a separate study suggest that if a person vaccinated with Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) undergoes a tuberculin skin test (TST) after exposure to Mycobacterium tuberculosis and the reaction size of the test increases by more than 15 mm in induration compared to a TST conducted prior to the exposure, this increase in size is likely indicative of a newly acquired M. tuberculosis infection. Tuberculin skin testing is not contraindicated for individuals who have received the BCG vaccine, and the results of such tests can be used to either support or exclude the diagnosis of M. tuberculosis infection. A diagnosis of M. tuberculosis infection and the initiation of preventive therapy should be considered for any BCG-vaccinated individual who has a TST reaction of ≥10 mm induration, particularly under the following circumstances: (a) the vaccinated individual has been in contact with someone who has infectious tuberculosis (TB), especially if the infectious person has transmitted M. tuberculosis to others, such as healthcare workers, employees and volunteers at homeless shelters, or workers at drug-treatment centers. Preventive therapy for TB should also be considered for BCG-vaccinated individuals infected with HIV who are at risk for M. tuberculosis infection if they have a TST reaction of ≥5 mm induration or if they are nonreactive to tuberculin. Nonreactivity to delayed-type hypersensitivity (DTH) antigens may occur before the onset of clinical signs and symptoms of HIV infection. The possibility of anergy in BCG-vaccinated individuals infected with HIV is supported by studies conducted in Rwanda, where all children are vaccinated with BCG. These studies demonstrated reduced tuberculin skin-test responses in HIV-infected children compared to uninfected children. Additionally, among BCG-vaccinated women in Uganda, those infected with HIV were more likely to be nonreactive to tuberculin compared to women in an HIV-seronegative control group. A diagnosis of active TB disease should be considered in BCG-vaccinated individuals, regardless of their TST results or HIV serostatus, if they exhibit symptoms suggestive of TB, particularly if they have had recent exposure to infectious TB. The primary strategy for controlling TB in the United States is to minimize the risk of transmission by promptly identifying and treating patients with active infectious TB. The secondary strategy involves identifying individuals with latent M. tuberculosis infection and, if indicated, administering preventive therapy with isoniazid to prevent the progression of latent infection to active TB disease. Rifampin is used for preventive therapy in individuals infected with isoniazid-resistant strains of M. tuberculosis. The use of the BCG vaccine has been limited due to two main reasons: (a) its uncertain effectiveness in preventing infectious forms of TB and (b) the interference of post-vaccination tuberculin reactivity with the management of individuals potentially infected with M. tuberculosis. The use of BCG vaccination as a TB prevention strategy is reserved for select individuals who meet specific criteria. In children, a diagnosis of TB is considered a sentinel event, indicating recent transmission of M. tuberculosis within the community. For instance, in one study, nearly all children infected with M. tuberculosis had acquired the infection from infected adults, many of whom resided in the same household as the child. These findings highlight the importance of promptly reporting TB cases to public health authorities and initiating thorough contact investigations to identify children at risk for TB infection and disease. The severity of active TB disease in childhood necessitates special efforts to protect children, particularly those under 5 years of age, from infection with M. tuberculosis. Children are primarily protected through the implementation of the first TB control strategy, which involves interrupting transmission by promptly identifying and treating individuals with infectious TB. In adults, nonadherence to prescribed TB treatment can result in prolonged infectiousness and increased transmission of M. tuberculosis. Directly observed therapy (DOT) is an effective method to ensure adherence and should be considered for all adult TB patients. If an infectious adult fails to comply with anti-TB therapy, public health authorities should consider removing any children from contact with the adult until the patient is no longer infectious. Unless specifically contraindicated, preventive therapy should be administered to all tuberculin-positive children, even if the date of skin-test conversion or the source of M. tuberculosis infection cannot be precisely determined.
